name: Floorp
summary: Open source browser built on Firefox, adding workspaces with container isolation, split view, web panels and interface customisation on top of the Gecko platform.

content.introduction:
Floorp is an open source web browser built on Firefox. Its own site states the position in one line — "an open source browser built on Firefox, with workspaces, split view, web panels, and more" — and the project's repository describes itself as "the most Advanced and Fastest Firefox derivative", a formula that belongs to the project rather than to an independent test.

The version landmark used here is 12.21.0, published on 27 October 2026. The release notes for that version state that the Firefox base has been updated to the 159 series, which is the clearest statement of the project's relationship to its upstream: Floorp follows Firefox releases and rebases onto them.

Floorp is a desktop browser for Windows, macOS and Linux, distributed as direct downloads, package-manager entries and a Flatpak, with an iOS version currently in testing through Apple's TestFlight. It requires no account to use, and its distinguishing features are organisational rather than engine-level: workspaces that group tabs, a split view that displays up to four pages at once, web panels in a sidebar, and a settings hub that exposes options Firefox does not.
content.origin_and_history:
The project's public history is short and can be dated from its own infrastructure. The GitHub repository that holds the source of Floorp 12 was created on 12 December 2021, and the source is published by the GitHub organisation `Floorp-Projects`. The repository description refers to "Floorp 12", which indicates that the current product line is version 12 and that earlier releases existed under the same name; the sources read do not document the numbered history before version 12 except through feature notes that reference it.

Those notes do give a few dated milestones. The documentation for workspaces states that the ability to pre-assign a Firefox Multi-Account Container to a workspace was introduced in Floorp 11.4.0, citing a project blog post dated 22 September 2023. The split view documentation states that, as of version 12.14.2, up to four tabs can be displayed simultaneously, and the workspaces documentation dates a change in how workspace structures are shared, across the same profile, to the same 12.14.2 release.

Recent releases are documented one by one on the project's blog: 12.20.0 on 8 October 2026, 12.20.1 on 9 October 2026, 12.20.2 on 17 October 2026, and 12.21.0 on 27 October 2026. The 12.21.0 notes describe a Firefox 159 base, synchronisation of workspaces and their tabs, and a list of bug fixes. No founding date for the project as a whole is published in the sources read, and this entry does not invent one.
content.rendering_engine_and_technical_architect:
Floorp does not build its own engine: it inherits Firefox's, and the release notes phrase this as a base update ("the Firefox base has been updated to the 159 series"). The repository's topics list `firefox`, `gecko` and `mozilla`, and the project's comparison table places Floorp next to Firefox on a line about open source code, which is consistent with a derivative that keeps the upstream engine and source licensing.

The practical architecture is therefore layered: Gecko renders pages, Firefox supplies the application shell, the extension system, the account integration and the update mechanism, and Floorp adds a layer of its own features — workspaces, split view, panels, the settings hub, notes, the command palette and web apps. The repository's primary language is listed as TypeScript, which fits that description: what the project writes is mostly browser interface code, not engine code.

Two consequences follow and are worth separating. First, web platform behaviour, extension compatibility and security patching come from Firefox, so a Floorp user tracks Firefox's release train indirectly, through Floorp's rebases. Second, features that touch the browser's internals — tab stacks, containers, panels, the sidebar — are the ones the project documents in detail, because they are the ones it owns.

Floorp also depends on Mozilla services for one documented feature: workspace and tab synchronisation uses a Mozilla Account, and its release notes describe precisely what is and is not transferred.
content.interface_and_documented_features:
The interface is Firefox's, extended. The site names four headline features: workspaces, which group tabs by task and can assign Firefox containers so that cookies and sign-ins stay separate; split view, which places several pages in one window with adjustable widths; web panels, which pin frequently used sites to the sidebar without leaving the current page; and interface customisation, including mouse gestures and web apps that open sites in their own windows.

The documentation adds detail on each. Workspaces can be created, renamed, archived and restored from a management panel reached through a toolbar button; only one workspace is shown per window at a time; tabs in inactive workspaces stay open in the background; and the settings for them live in Floorp Hub, an internal page reachable at `about:hub`, which also holds the option to list workspaces in the panel sidebar. Split view builds on Firefox's native split view and extends it: adding further panes by right-clicking a tab already in split view, up to four tabs as of 12.14.2, and dragging a tab into the page area to split top, bottom, left or right, with a drop in the centre moving the tab to a new window instead.

The 12.21.0 release notes name further features in passing, through the fixes applied to them: Tab Stacks with a minimum tab width setting, a command palette, a status bar, web apps on Windows, Floorp Start, and Notes, which gained Markdown export in the 12.20.0 cycle and whose synchronisation is repaired in 12.21.0. The notes also introduce synchronisation of selected workspaces and their tabs across Floorp installations that use the same Mozilla Account, excluding private windows, local files and internal browser pages, and explicitly not synchronising form contents, cookies or container assignments.

The site is also careful about one point that matters for evaluation: it publishes a comparison table with other browsers on container isolation tied to workspaces, splitting three or more pages in one window, built-in web panels and open source code, and links each claim to a source. That table is the project's own argument, not an independent test.
content.installation_and_distribution:
Download routes are documented per platform. On Windows, the download page offers an online installer described as recommended, an offline installer, a `winget` package and a portable edition; the installation documentation gives the command `winget install Ablaze.Floorp` and a Scoop bucket route, both attributed to named contributors. On macOS, a universal DMG is the recommended route and Homebrew is offered as an alternative; the documentation describes dragging `Floorp.app` into the Applications folder. On Linux, the documented options are a tarball for x86_64 and one for AArch64, a DEB package for Debian and Ubuntu, a Flatpak from Flathub, and a PPA for Ubuntu and Linux Mint; the installation documentation adds unofficial AUR and SlackBuild packages and warns that the Flatpak sandbox imposes its own limitations.

Integrity information is published: the download page states that releases are served from GitHub Releases, that Windows installers are code-signed, that the macOS application is notarized by Apple, and that SHA-256 hashes are provided for verification. GitHub Releases also hosts previous versions, which the documentation says are downloadable but no longer supported.

The installation page defines two channel names that are easy to confuse. Floorp Daylight is now the name of the debug build for developers, having previously been the name of the public beta. Experimental features now reach the stable build through a progressive rollout system called Floorp Flasco, which the documentation presents as the reason a separate beta browser is no longer needed.

No store-based mobile installation is documented; the iOS version is described as being tested through TestFlight.
content.platforms_and_hardware_architectures:
Three desktop platforms are documented, with explicit minimums. On Windows: Windows 11 and Windows 10, both 64-bit, a processor supporting SSE4.1, 2 GB of RAM and 200 MB of free space. On macOS: macOS Catalina 10.15 through macOS Sequoia 15, on Intel or Apple Silicon, with 512 MB of RAM and 200 MB of free space; the distributed disk image is universal. On Linux: x86_64 or AArch64, with GTK+ 3.14 or higher and glibc 2.17 or higher required, plus X.org 1.0 or higher and libstdc++ 4.8.1 or higher; NetworkManager, DBus, GNOME, PulseAudio are listed as recommended for best functionality.

Those requirements match the published artefacts. The latest release publishes a universal macOS image, a Windows stub installer, and Linux packages for x86_64 and AArch64 in the form of tarballs and a Debian package, which is why the entry lists both architectures for Linux.

Mobile coverage is partial and documented as such: the site states that Floorp for iOS is currently being tested through TestFlight. No Android build appears in the sources read, and this entry records that absence rather than inferring a roadmap.

Beyond these minimums, the project publishes no hardware acceleration requirements or recommended configuration in the sources read; the sensible reading is that the browser inherits Firefox's platform expectations, which the project does not restate.
content.extensions_and_add_on_store:
Floorp inherits Firefox's extension system, and its documentation leans on that inheritance rather than describing a catalogue of its own: the split view and workspaces pages refer readers to Mozilla's support documentation for the underlying Firefox features and for containers. The repository's topics include `mozilla` and `firefox`, and the project's comparison table treats extension availability as a property of the Firefox base rather than as a Floorp-specific marketplace.

What Floorp adds is partly built in rather than installed: workspaces, split view, panels, mouse gestures, web apps, tab stacks and the command palette are documented as browser features, not as add-ons. The release notes also mention fixes involving "Chrome extension prompts" in the 12.20.2 cycle, which indicates that Firefox's compatibility layer for Chromium-style extensions is in use in the product; the sources read do not elaborate on how far that compatibility extends.

No Floorp-operated store, review process or extension count is documented. This entry therefore claims only that the Firefox extension mechanism is inherited, that some Chromium-style extension prompts are handled, and that core features are built in. Anyone evaluating a specific add-on should verify it rather than assume compatibility from the browser's Firefox base alone.
content.privacy_and_security_model:
The project presents privacy as a matter of choice rather than of a fixed policy: its front page lists "Privacy is your choice" as one of three headline claims, alongside open source status and the Firefox base. The documentation read does not publish a telemetry inventory, a data collection statement or an independent audit, so this entry makes no claim about what the browser sends and when.

What is documented is the point where data leaves the machine. Workspace and tab synchronisation, introduced in 12.21.0, transfers selected workspaces — names, icons and web tabs — to other Floorp installations that sync with the same Mozilla Account. The release notes state the exclusions explicitly: private windows, local files and internal browser pages are not synchronised, and form contents, cookies and container assignments are not synchronised either. Nothing is uploaded until a workspace is explicitly selected for synchronisation, and a status indicator shows which workspaces are selected. That is a documented design, and it also states the limit of the guarantee: the data path runs through Mozilla's account service.

Security properties that the sources do state are distribution properties: Windows installers are code-signed, the macOS application is notarized by Apple, and SHA-256 hashes are published for verification. Because the engine and the update mechanism come from Firefox, engine-level security fixes arrive through Floorp's rebases onto new Firefox series, which the release notes date — the 159 series in 12.21.0, the 158 series in 12.20.2 and the 157.0.1 base in 12.20.0.

Three reservations apply. The project's privacy claim is a positioning, not a measurement. The container isolation that workspaces can use comes from Firefox's Multi-Account Containers, so its guarantees are Mozilla's. And a browser rebased onto upstream releases inherits upstream's choices, so a Floorp user is affected by Firefox's defaults as well as by Floorp's additions.
content.update_channels_and_release_cadence:
Two channel concepts are documented and one of them changed meaning. The stable channel is the standard release published on the site and on GitHub Releases, currently 12.21.0 dated 27 October 2026. Floorp Daylight, formerly the public beta build, is now described as the debug build for developers. Experimental features reach stable through Floorp Flasco, a progressive rollout system, which the documentation presents as replacing the need for a separate beta browser.

The cadence is fast and follows upstream. The blog dates 12.20.0 on 8 October 2026, 12.20.1 on 9 October 2026, 12.20.2 on 17 October 2026 and 12.21.0 on 27 October 2026 — four releases in under three weeks — and each of those versions is tied to a Firefox base: 157.0.1, then 158, then 159. Patch releases appear within days of each other when a regression matters, as 12.20.1 did after 12.20.0.

The update experience is visible in the notes rather than described as a policy: the 12.21.0 fixes include honouring the user's choice not to open release notes automatically after an update, and avoiding opening both the blog home page and the version's notes when automatic opening is enabled. That documents an in-product update flow with release notes, without publishing a support window for older versions; the download page states only that previous versions have a different support status from the current stable release.
content.licensing_and_governance:
The repository is published under the Mozilla Public License 2.0, according to the licence metadata exposed by GitHub for `Floorp-Projects/Floorp`. That licence is the same family as Firefox's, which is consistent with a derivative that keeps upstream code and publishes its own additions; the project's comparison table presents open source code as one of its differentiators against browsers that publish only part of their code.

Governance is that of a small open source project organised around a GitHub organisation rather than a foundation. The source, releases, issues and discussions are hosted in `Floorp-Projects`; bug reports and feature requests are directed to GitHub Issues; support channels listed in the documentation are Discord, X, Reddit and Misskey. The site publishes a donation page, including a route through Stripe that the 12.21.0 notes describe as requiring no Floorp account.

Scale indicators are public and date-stamped on the repository: at the time of writing the repository showed more than 8,400 stars, more than 280 forks, 120 open issues and 38 watchers, with the last push on 29 October 2026. Those figures measure attention, not quality, but they do establish that the project is active and that its issue tracker is a live channel rather than an archive.

Two consequences for readers: the project is not backed by a foundation comparable to Mozilla or GNOME, so its continuity rests on its own contributors and donations; and its licence covers its own code while the Firefox base keeps upstream licensing, so the software freedom of the whole depends on both.
content.limitations_and_scope:
The first limitation is structural: Floorp is a derivative, so its web platform, extension behaviour and security patching follow Firefox releases. The release notes show the dependency plainly, naming the Firefox series adopted at each version. A Floorp feature can therefore lag a Firefox change, and an upstream change can arrive in Floorp only at the next rebase.

The second limitation concerns documented coverage. The sources read publish no telemetry statement, no independent security audit and no support window for older versions. They describe the synchronisation feature in detail, including what it excludes, but not a general privacy policy. This entry records those gaps as undocumented rather than as absent.

The third concerns scope of distribution. Desktop coverage is documented for Windows 10 and 11 on 64-bit, macOS 10.15 and later, and Linux on x86_64 and AArch64; iOS is in TestFlight testing; no Android build appears in the sources read. Some Linux routes are explicitly unofficial — AUR and SlackBuild packages — and the Flatpak build is documented as carrying sandbox limitations.

Finally, the project's claims are its own. The comparison table on the site compares Floorp with Chrome, Firefox and Vivaldi on four features and links each cell to a source, but it is a vendor comparison, not a benchmark; this entry reports it as such and reports no performance measurement of its own.
content.who_is_it_for: Floorp suits Firefox users who want organisational tools the upstream browser does not provide — workspaces with container isolation, a split view for up to four pages, a panel sidebar, tab stacks, a command palette and a settings hub — while keeping the Gecko engine, Firefox's extension ecosystem and the Firefox account for optional synchronisation. It suits people who work across several contexts on one machine and want the contexts separated, and those who prefer built-in features to installing add-ons.
content.who_is_it_not_for: It is not aimed at users who need a browser independent of Firefox's release train: Floorp rebases onto Firefox series and inherits its platform and patch timing. It is not for anyone requiring a published privacy policy, telemetry inventory or independent audit, none of which appears in the sources read. It is not a mobile browser yet outside an iOS TestFlight, and no Android build is documented. It is not an anonymity tool, and its synchronisation feature depends on a Mozilla Account.
content.verdict: Floorp is best understood as a Firefox derivative that invests in tab organisation rather than in engine work. The documentation establishes the essentials: a Firefox 159 base in version 12.21.0 published on 27 October 2026, workspaces with container assignment, split view extended to four panes, web panels, a settings hub at `about:hub`, optional workspace and tab synchronisation through a Mozilla Account with its exclusions stated, MPL-2.0 licensing, signed Windows installers, a notarized macOS image and published hashes. It also establishes the shape of the trade-off: a small project with a fast rebase cadence, no foundation behind it, no published privacy statement, and a dependency on upstream for the engine and its patches. That combination is coherent for the users it targets — people who want more organisation than Firefox offers without leaving Gecko — and it is why the entry documents the base version and the exclusions of each feature rather than the project's own superlatives.
